content:
What CamWallet is CamWallet is a platform at TSC for government benefit schemes. A scheme owner, usually a ministry or agency, funds a programme and decides who receives value. Beneficiaries spend that value with approved merchants. CamWallet holds the value, checks each payment when it happens, and keeps a record good enough to reconcile and audit.
There are three surfaces. Scheme owners and merchants use a Back Office portal built with Nuxt 4. Beneficiaries pay through the CamDigiKey app, which is Cambodia’s digital identity app. Merchants accept payments in a native Flutter Merchant App. The backend is Java 25 on Spring Boot 4.1 with Spring Modulith, Spring Data JDBC and Postgres.
v2 is two changes, not a rewrite Version 1 worked like this.
A scheme defined eligibility rules, and CamWallet decided who qualified. People who qualified received value in a wallet. They paid merchants through a bank, using Bakong, ABA or ACLEDA. The bank confirmed the payment, and CamWallet recorded the outcome. Version 2 changes the first and third steps. The scheme owner now decides who qualifies in their own system, and CamWallet records that decision without re-checking it. Payment now happens inside CamWallet, between a beneficiary’s value and a merchant’s balance, with no bank in the path.
Everything else carries over, including the double-entry ledger, CamDigiKey login, disbursement scheduling, idempotency and the audit trail. That is why we treated v2 as a milestone on the existing codebase rather than a new system. When we wrote down the full v1-to-v2 delta, it came to ten rows: four additions, three deletions, two renames and one re-point.
Why the two changes cascade Each change removes a lot of machinery.
Once the scheme owner decides eligibility, CamWallet doesn’t need eligibility attributes, a registry lookup or an approval workflow. The schemes/eligibility/ module goes away. Eligibility evaluation, merchant vetting and base-registry integration are now permanently out of scope.
Once payment is internal, merchants need a balance, so each merchant gets a ledger account. The money is owed to the merchant until the scheme owner pays them outside the system, so settlement has to debit that balance. The payment-gateway clients for the banks have nothing left to do and are deleted.
The design rests on one sentence. A scheme owner funds a programme and decides who qualifies, and CamWallet makes sure the money is only spent with approved merchants and then tells the owner exactly what to pay each merchant.
The ledger Everything is a transfer between two accounts. Entries are appended and never changed, and every balance can be explained by replaying its entries. Reconciliation becomes arithmetic instead of investigation.
Account What it holds scheme:{id}:expenditure Total ever granted in the scheme grant:{id} One grant’s unspent value payable:{scheme}:{merchant} What the scheme owes one merchant scheme:{id}:paid_out Total recorded as paid to merchants scheme:{id}:returned Unspent value from expired grants Each enrolment is a grant with its own amount and validity dates, and a beneficiary can hold several. A wallet is not an account. It is the set of a beneficiary’s grant accounts in one scheme, and its spendable balance only counts grants that are valid today.
Payables are per scheme. A merchant serving two schemes has two payables, because each scheme settles separately and the obligations must not pool.
Operation From → To Disburse scheme expenditure → grant Pay grant (soonest end date first) → payable Record payout payable → scheme paid_out Return expired value grant → scheme returned A payment that draws on two grants writes two debits and one credit in one transaction. Because expenditure moves only on disbursement, reconciliation is a single identity per scheme that we can check in one query and assert in a test.
granted = Σ grant balances + Σ payables + paid_out + returned Making it safe in Postgres Removing the bank removed the distributed transaction. A payment debits grant accounts and credits a payable in one ACID transaction inside one database. There is no two-phase commit and no compensating action. That single fact made the rest of the design much simpler.
A few rules keep the ledger honest.
Entries are immutable. A database trigger rejects UPDATE and DELETE on ledger_entries. A correction is a new reversing entry. Cached balances change atomically. Grant and payable accounts cache their balance, because payment checks read those two numbers. The cache only changes inside one posting method, as SET balance = balance + :delta. A read-modify-write in Java isn’t allowed, because many wallets credit the same payable at once. A test asserts that each cached balance equals the sum of its entries. Every transfer balances. The posting code rejects an unbalanced set of entries before it writes anything. Locks guard the checks, not the arithmetic. A payment locks the beneficiary’s wallet row before it reads any grant. A payment from a dynamic QR locks the QR first, so one QR can’t be paid twice. Credits need no lock, because the atomic delta already makes them safe. Money is exact decimal. Amounts are numeric(19,4) and always travel with their currency. A posting across two currencies is rejected. Declines have a closed vocabulary Every declined payment carries exactly one reason code from a fixed list, evaluated in a fixed order. The list includes QR_REVOKED, QR_ALREADY_PAID, QR_EXPIRED, MERCHANT_INACTIVE, NO_SCHEME_AT_MERCHANT, MERCHANT_NOT_PARTICIPATING, CREDIT_NOT_YET_VALID, CREDIT_EXPIRED and INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE.
Adding a code later is cheap. Rewriting months of free-text rejection messages into something a report can group is not.
What it removed from the build The original 2026 proposal named Postgres, MinIO and Kafka. For a four-week build at pilot volume, Postgres covers most of that list. It holds the ledger, configuration, audit trail and Spring Modulith’s event publication registry. Each piece of infrastructure we didn’t add is one fewer thing to deploy, monitor and explain to the next developer.
Merchant QRs A recent piece of work let merchants manage their own static QRs. A merchant often takes payments at more than one counter, and each counter needs its own printed QR with a label so staff and payers know where it belongs. A QR names the merchant, currency and label but no scheme, and the beneficiary picks the scheme when they pay.
The EMV QR format limits the merchant name in tag 59 to 25 characters. We had been filling it from the merchant’s English name, which had no length limit. Merchants now get a separate display name capped at 25 printable ASCII characters, and that name is what appears on the QR.
Looking back The most useful document in the project is one page called “What v2 actually is.” It lists the four steps, marks the two that changed, and traces every other decision back to them. New readers start there. When a design discussion drifted, we went back to that page and asked which of the two changes the proposal followed from. If it followed from neither, it usually belonged in a later phase.
summary: How CamWallet’s second version changed two assumptions, who decides eligibility and where payment happens, and why everything else in the design follows from those two changes.
title: CamWallet v2: A Closed Ledger With No Bank in the Path

content:
The setup For CamWallet v2 I drove implementation through the BMad Method and a CLI called bmad-loop. BMad is a set of AI agent skills for planning, writing stories, implementing and reviewing. bmad-loop runs the implementation phase unattended. It picks the next story from a sprint file, writes a spec, implements it, runs a verify gate and moves on. Our verify gate was a backend compile plus a frontend typecheck.
I ran retrospectives after Epic 1 (merchant management) and Epic 3 (scheme participation). Both epics shipped and both were accepted. Both retrospectives also found the same problem from different directions, so I’m writing them up together.
Epic 1: built, then removed Epic 1 had seven stories. The unattended run implemented all of them, along with seven capabilities that a pilot didn’t need. These included member management, a module API, an idempotency key, a member National ID field, server-side search and paging, merchant status and reference uniqueness.
Human review took them back out. The squashed feature commit was about 2,500 lines. After the slim-down, the net change against dev was about 550 lines across 13 files. Tests dominated the churn. One service test file gained 1,482 lines and lost 1,322.
Each removed capability became a tracked deferral, so the work wasn’t wasted as a record of intent. It was wasted as build time and review time.
The retrospective produced four process lessons.
Slim the scope before building, not after. Before the next run, I would mark each story’s pilot-minimal scope and its deferrals in the epic context file, and apply a minimal-test rule of one service test per rule and one controller test per route. The loop’s independent review never ran. It was set to trigger only when recommended, and no pass recommended it. Every defect in Epic 1 was found by a human. I had to decide whether to make the loop review always or keep human review as the gate on purpose. Don’t rewrite history during review. I squashed and force-pushed while the PR was open, and the commit references in our docs moved six times. During review I should add commits and squash once, at merge. Clean up after the run. Archive the paused run and mark the epic done in the sprint file. Epic 3: same pattern, smaller Epic 3 was smaller, with three stories and a net change of 4 files and about 224 added lines. I had applied the Epic 1 lessons, so I expected a clean run. It wasn’t clean.
About 250 lines landed on dev and never survived. One story added a custom JSON deserializer and the next story removed it. A 104-line controller test grew to 151 lines and was then deleted by a refactor commit. The retrospective traced this to five causes.
The epic started on a stale base. dev had already gained a component that did the deserializer’s job, but the plan still said to build one, and the agent followed the plan. It built what the plan described without checking what the code already did. “Minimal tests” failed in both directions. The first pass wrote about 480 test lines despite the rule. The trim then cut too deep and dropped the only assertions that checked membership and roles. The rule said how many tests to write but not which ones mattered. Memory pressure killed the run twice. Each kill needed a manual rollback. Accepting the committed work as a new baseline then mismatched the spec’s recorded baseline, so the loop deferred a story that was already finished. A proposal encoded a wrong framework assumption. It planned to catch a wrapped DbActionExecutionException, but Spring Data JDBC throws DuplicateKeyException directly. The test suite caught it. Four course-correction proposals in two days reshaped one small epic. The merged commits didn’t line up with story boundaries. The pattern Both retrospectives show an agent loop that is good at producing code that matches a plan and poor at noticing when the plan is out of date. It doesn’t push back on scope, so it builds everything the plan mentions. It doesn’t check the current branch, so it rebuilds things that already exist. It treats a test-count rule as a quota rather than a judgement about risk.
None of these are coding failures. The code compiled, the tests passed and the reviews found real but ordinary defects. The cost came from building the wrong amount of the right thing.
What I’m changing The lessons point at how I prepare work, not at how the loop runs.
Write the scope down before the run. Each story should list what the pilot needs and what is deferred, so the agent can’t build past it without contradicting an explicit line. Name tests by risk instead of counting them. The backend instructions now say not to test CRUD round-trips or simple 404s. Tests that protect tenancy are different. A cross-organisation request must return 404, and a non-member must be forbidden on every scheme route. Check the plan against dev first. A plan written a week ago can describe code that someone has since merged. Epic 4 opened with a story that restored the membership and role tests the Epic 3 trim had dropped, and added a payable-currency check. Even that story went through one more round of cutting. It added a 404 test for an unknown ID and then removed it before merge, because the lean-test rule says simple 404s aren’t worth a test. The cross-organisation 404s stayed, because they protect tenancy. I think that’s the rule working as intended. The line between the two cases is now written down, so the agent and I don’t have to argue it from scratch each time.
Reflection An unattended loop makes it cheap to produce code and expensive to produce the wrong amount of it. Most of my judgement as the engineer now goes into what happens before the run. I decide what the pilot needs, which tests protect something real, and whether the plan still matches the code. When I did that work up front, the loop’s output needed little review. When I skipped it, I spent the review deleting code.
summary: CamWallet’s v2 epics were built with an unattended AI agent loop. Two retrospectives showed the same pattern each time: the loop built too much, a human review cut it back, and the history recorded both.
title: CamWallet: What Two Retrospectives Taught Me About Building With an Agent Loop

content:
Background ESB stands for E-Services for Business. It is a Royal Government of Cambodia programme that gives ministries a shared foundation for digital public services. The flow is the same for most of them. A business submits an application, an officer reviews it, the business pays, and the ministry issues a certificate. At TSC (Techo Startup Center) we maintain an open generic template for this, and each ministry gets its own instance.
I work on the MOT instance, for the Ministry of Tourism. Its first licences cover restaurants, accommodation, sport venues and tour agents. MOT was forked from the agriculture instance, so the code still carries farm-licence names like FarmType and FarmSize. I learned early to read those as inherited scaffolding rather than intent.
The workspace is about twenty independent GitHub repos checked out side by side. Each service, portal, shared library and infrastructure repo has its own trunk, version and release cycle. A change that touches three services means three coordinated commits, and often a library version bump and a Helm chart bump on top.
This post follows one restaurant registration from the form to the PDF. I wrote the original trace for a teammate coming from Rails, and it turned out to be the most useful document I produced this year.
The shape of it A restaurant owner fills in a form and picks a seating-capacity band, which is also the fee line item. They submit it. New applications must be paid before an officer ever sees them. That rule comes from a global PAYMENT_MODE switch, which selects pay-first-review-later or review-first-pay-later for the whole platform. Changing it changes the application lifecycle, not just a label.
An officer reviews and approves the application in review-service. Approval fires a Kafka message that profile-service consumes to create the licence record. Profile-service then asks certificate-service to render the PDF.
In Rails this would be one controller and an after_commit callback. Here it is five Spring Boot processes, three databases and two Kafka hops, and no single log file shows the whole story.
restaurant form (Nuxt public portal) → repositories/application/request-application.repo.ts → server/api/[...].ts (Nitro proxy) → public-gateway-service (Spring Cloud Gateway) → application-service (save, then submit) → Kafka: application_submitted_message → review-service (officer approves) → Kafka: review_request_created_message → application-service (marks approved) → Kafka: application_approved_message → profile-service (creates the licence) → certificate-service (renders the PDF) Hop by hop The portal never calls a backend directly Every endpoint lives in a repositories/*.ts file, and plugins/api.ts registers each repository on one shared fetcher. That fetcher attaches auth headers and handles the response envelope in one place. A repository file that exists but is not registered is unreachable. You get undefined is not a function instead of a 404, and this is the most common reason a new endpoint “doesn’t work.”
The request then goes to the portal’s own Nitro server. A catch-all route at server/api/[...].ts rewrites /api/** to the gateway URL and turns the httpOnly access_token cookie into a Bearer header. The browser never sees a backend address.
Gateway routes are Java classes Spring Cloud Gateway can be configured in YAML, but ours isn’t. Each downstream service has a *RouteConfiguration class with path predicates, a token-requirement filter and an authorization filter. If you add an endpoint and forget the route class, the gateway returns 404 and the service never sees the request. This failure mode comes up often enough that I now check the route class before I check anything else.
application-service dispatches on a service code Every licence type has a service code, and GDTI-RT-L is a new restaurant licence. ApplicationStrategyFactory builds a map from service code to strategy bean, so a restaurant application ends up in TourismRestaurantLicenseStrategy. Renewal, amendment, transfer and termination each get their own strategy. Adding a licence type means adding strategies rather than editing a growing switch.
Kafka messages go out after the commit Business code never calls a Kafka producer directly. It publishes a Spring domain event such as ApplicationSubmittedDomainEvent, and a @TransactionalEventListener sends the Kafka message after the database transaction commits. A rolled-back submission therefore can’t leak a message that tells review-service to start work on a row that doesn’t exist.
Schemas live in one repo The Avro .avsc files live in infrastructure/schema-registry, not in the services. Each service lists the subjects it needs in its pom.xml, and the build downloads them from the Schema Registry and generates Java classes. A service won’t compile without a reachable registry. It also needs the KAFKA_TENANT_ID_PREFIX variable exported, even when the prefix is empty.
I lost an afternoon to the tenant prefix. The publisher adds the trailing dot itself, so passing esb. produces subjects named esb..application_submitted_message-value. Every service build then 404s on its subject, and the error message points at the registry rather than at the double dot.
Same class name, different repo Profile-service has its own TourismRestaurantLicenseStrategy. It has the same name as the one in application-service, lives in a different repo, and does a different job. The application-service strategy validates and stores the application. The profile-service one turns an approved application into a licence. Searching the workspace for the class name returns both, and new readers routinely open the wrong one.
The certificate Certificate-service renders the licence through jsreport with Khmer fonts and templates. The official MOT tourism licence also carries a verification QR, which anyone can scan to confirm the licence is genuine through verify.gov. Most of the code for that already existed when I picked it up. The restaurant certificate row was seeded with verification switched off, so the QR block never rendered. Turning it on was mostly a matter of wiring up external endpoints and credentials and removing configuration that the code never read.
What differs for the other operations Registration is the longest path, so I traced it first. The other four operations reuse most of the chain.
Renewal runs a rule engine before it bills. The engine is versioned and editable in the backoffice, and it can add a late-renewal penalty that payment-service prints as a bilingual invoice line. Amendment can change the licensee, address, restaurant details and inspection. It can’t change the capacity band, because the band is the fee. A licensee who needs a different band has to terminate and register again. Transfer looks up the recipient’s identity before profile-service moves the licence. Termination doesn’t issue a new certificate. It revokes the existing one. Transfer and termination skip the payment gate entirely and go straight to officer review. Eligibility is enforced by the same rule engine. An expired licence can’t be amended or transferred, a terminated one can’t be renewed, and a licence can’t be terminated twice. Restaurant supplies these rules as configuration rows rather than code.
What I’d tell someone starting on it Read one flow end to end before you change anything. The services are small and conventional on their own. The difficulty is at the joints between them, which are gateway routes, Avro subjects, Kafka topics and the department header that the backoffice portal sends on every request. Most of the bugs I fixed this year sat on one of those joints. The next post covers how we started testing them.
summary: Tracing a single restaurant licence application through the Ministry of Tourism’s ESB platform, from a Nuxt form to a signed PDF, across five Spring Boot services and two Kafka hops.
title: ESB-MOT: One Restaurant Licence, Five Services

content:
Where we started The MOT platform ships through about twenty independent repos that talk to each other over two gateways and Avro messages on Kafka. In October 2026, no test ran in CI, and the Jenkins builds skipped tests. Many test files existed on developers’ machines but had never been committed, because a local exclude kept src/test out of git.
On 2026-10-19 I brought the existing tests under version control. The baseline that day was red in 15 of 16 Maven repos and in both portals, and 23 test classes didn’t compile at all against the current code.
That number sounds bad, but it was useful. It told us the tests had drifted from the code for months without anyone noticing, which is exactly what happens when nothing runs them.
Defects live at the boundaries Before writing a strategy, I looked at what actually broke on our dev environment. The defects clustered in four places, and per-class unit tests catch none of them.
Unrouted gateway paths. A portal calls an endpoint the gateway has no route for, and the request 404s before it reaches the service. Schema mismatches. A producer and consumer disagree about an Avro field or a union default. Department-scope 403s. A guarded endpoint rejects a user who should have access, or accepts one who shouldn’t. Seed-data drift. A seeder inserts duplicate keys, or a fee row is missing a revenue code that the ministry’s workbook says should exist. The developers maintaining MOT, including me, were finding these by hand during smoke passes, one at a time.
Re-verifying the bug ledger We keep a ledger of deferred defects. Someone writes an entry when they find a problem, and nobody revisits it afterwards. By September there were 26 open entries marked high severity. I checked every one against the current code and the live local databases instead of trusting the entry text.
Outcome Count Stale, already fixed by later work 4 Fixed and shipped the same day 2 Confirmed real and reachable 11 Real, fix written but parked 1 Real but not reachable today 3 Real but deliberate design 1 Not verified 3 External, not an engineering task 1 Four entries described problems that no longer existed. Several of the confirmed ones had a different cause from the one recorded. One “small data task” turned out to need an ownership ruling from the ministry and a code change, because the penalty revenue code was derived as serviceCode + "-PENALTY". That formula can’t tell two seating-capacity bands apart, and the ministry bills them under different treasury codes.
My conclusion is that a defect ledger rots like any other documentation. An entry records what someone believed on the day they wrote it. It needs re-verification before anyone plans work from it.
The stale department header One bug shows the boundary problem clearly. Backoffice staff would occasionally open the applications list and get a 403 with the message key unable.to.view.applications.from.other.departments, even though they belonged to the department they were viewing.
The cause was in the portal, not the backend. A user’s permissions are scoped to a department, and the portal sends an X-Department-ID header on every request. The selected department lived in a module-scope ref, which is a singleton for the whole app rather than per login. It was also persisted under one fixed localStorage key that wasn’t tied to any user.
A watcher auto-selected the first department for a newly loaded user, but only when nothing was selected yet. If the previous user’s department was still in localStorage, the watcher never fired. The new user’s departments loaded correctly but were never applied, and every request went out with someone else’s department ID.
The stored value was only cleared on the explicit Logout menu action. A failed token refresh, a redirect from the auth middleware, or a closed browser all skipped it.
The backend did its job by refusing a department the user didn’t belong to. The bug was a correct server-side check receiving a stale client-side header. Reproducing it was harder than explaining it. The obvious reproduction is two real CamDigiKey logins in one browser, but we had no local CamDigiKey mock and only one working identity. The auth cookies are httpOnly and secure, so no tool could inject a second user’s session without adding a bypass route to the portal, and we ruled that out. The reproduction became a test against the composable itself. It puts a stale department in localStorage, gives the composable a different user’s department list, and asserts that the header value changes. It needs no login, cookie or browser, and the same test serves as the regression check for the fix.
The strategy The testing strategy assigns each recurring defect class to the cheapest test layer that catches it.
Offline fast tests per service. Unit and slice tests run with Schema Registry and Docker stopped. Anything that needs a database or Kafka is tagged and runs in a separate tier. Message-contract checks. The schema publisher refuses an incompatible change to a field or union default. A producer whose serialized message no longer matches its registered subject fails a round-trip test, with or without the tenant prefix. Gateway route coverage. Removing a path from a route class, or adding a portal call with no matching route, fails a check. Real-database persistence tests. Repository, Specification and native SQL queries run against real Postgres through Testcontainers. A mocked repository would pass a broken column name. A real database won’t. Authorization and department-scope tests. Guarded endpoints are verified for each relevant role and department. The order matters. The first layer has to exist before anything goes into CI, because a suite that needs a running registry to compile can’t run on a Jenkins agent that has none. One service, nrmis-service, couldn’t even build in CI. Its pom.xml pulled Avro schemas from a sibling checkout that existed only on one developer’s laptop, so it had no Jenkins job and ArgoCD deployed nothing for it.
What I took from it Unit test coverage was never the main gap. Most of the classes we tested were simple and correct. The defects that hurt us came from two correct pieces that disagreed, such as a portal and a gateway, a producer and a consumer, or a seeder and a ministry spreadsheet. A strategy for a platform like this has to start from where the defects actually landed, and on MOT that was the joints between repos.
summary: MOT had no tests running in CI, and the defects that reached dev clustered at the boundaries between services. Notes on re-verifying a stale bug ledger, a stale department header, and a testing strategy built around where defects actually land.
title: ESB-MOT: Testing a Platform Spread Across Twenty Repos

content:
Background SAAMBAT is a Cambodia-government program supporting agricultural value chains, and KAS is the digital platform behind it. I’ve been working on it at TSC (Techo Startup Center). The platform grew organically over a few years — the kind of growth that ships features but accumulates the usual debts: a Node.js gateway no one fully owned, encryption layered between services that never left the cluster, two separate role tables, and a logging story that depended on whichever engineer set up the service first.
We kicked off a re-engineering program on 2026-01-01 with a clear scope for Phase 1: stop bleeding before adding any new industries. This post is a personal write-up of what shipped between January and the end of April.
The five things that mattered 1. The gateway is now Spring Cloud Gateway The old kas-core was a Node.js proxy doing JWT validation, partner E2EE, and routing. We replaced it with Spring Cloud Gateway on port 3000, with JWT validation moved to the edge using HS256 with a secret shared with kas-iam. Downstream services now verify locally; the /authenticate-jwt round-trip is gone.
Path rewriting is split cleanly: /api/* for internal traffic, /integrations/* for partners. CORS is centralized — localhost only allowed in non-prod profiles, and the Helm chart defaults to the prod Spring profile as a fail-safe.
It’s running in dev. Staging and production are waiting on DevOps to provision the new cluster.
2. We removed internal end-to-end encryption This one took some convincing. The previous design had secp256k1 + AES-256-CBC between every internal service. For traffic that never leaves the cluster, the operational complexity was real and the threat model was thin.
So we ripped it out internally and kept partner-facing E2EE, which we moved out of kas-core and into kas-service-registry — that’s where partner key material already lives. The @kas/e2ee-utils package stays for partner integrations.
Net effect: simpler internal topology, partner trust boundary unchanged.
3. IAM and RBAC, finally consolidated The single biggest defect I personally worked on was a duplicate-roles bug. Migration 001 had created agriculture-scoped roles without removing pre-existing duplicates. The result: createUser validation broke in surprising ways. Migration 003 deduplicates the roles, and createUser now runs Set-based dedup as defense in depth.
Auditing the permission model produced a useful surprise: per-service permission tables were dead data. The frontends drive authorization off roles, not individual permissions. Only USER.* permissions were actually enforced anywhere. So those tables go on the housekeeping pile.
Two smaller fixes in the same pass — the kas-iam Dockerfile now ships the public/ directory (email templates), and EmailController no longer crashes when a template file is missing.
4. Observability — one pattern, every service We picked a single transformation pattern and applied it everywhere:
Winston structured (JSON) logs Correlation IDs end-to-end (HTTP X-Correlation-ID, plus the Socket.io equivalent) Sentry for errors Slack alerting for 5xx with full context ELK for centralized log aggregation All eight backend services are on the pattern. Some are further along on OpenAPI documentation and Vitest coverage than others — kas-iam (43 endpoints), kas-service-registry (13), and kas-weather-api (107) are documented; others still need that pass.
5. Kafka as the event backbone Kafka 3.6, three brokers, KRaft mode (no ZooKeeper). 26 topics across portal, chat, notification, weather, resource, IAM, registry, and DLQ categories. Naming standardized as kas.<service>.<entity>.<event-type>. A kafka-init service auto-creates topics on startup; validate-topics.sh for health checks. Schema Registry 7.5.0 deployed (though contracts are not yet enforced — a known gap). Four DLQ topics in place; replay tooling is still manual, which is on the Phase-2 list. Local development that doesn’t fight you A small thing that mattered a lot: the unified Docker Compose stack in kas-infrastructure/. One command brings up MongoDB replica set, Redis, Kafka cluster, Schema Registry, ELK, and all eight backend services on documented ports. start.sh has --build and --no-cache flags; reset.sh got a --deep.
We also renamed docker-compose.override.yml → docker-compose.staging.yml. The old name was an automatic include — local dev was occasionally pointing at the staging MongoDB by accident. Now staging is opt-in via --staging.
Notable bugs along the way BUG-3 (form-data on kas-resource-api): farmer / family-member submissions were broken. Root cause was formidable 2.1.5 auto-parsing bracket notation while our manual reconstruction code did the same job — they fought. kas-weather-api: form handlers now have a fallback path, and error responses no longer leak internals. What’s left for Phase 1 These are operational, not architectural:
DevOps to provision the new cluster so the gateway can promote dev → staging → production. Once production cuts over, the legacy /authenticate-jwt endpoint can be retired. Housekeeping: sunset kas-core images and CI jobs, drop dead per-service permission tables, remove unused backend routes catalogued in docs/re-architecture/unused-backend-routes.md, scrub kas-core references from service CLAUDE.md files. What we’d need for nation-wide scale Phase 1 got us internally consistent. Going from there to production-grade for a nation-wide rollout is a different list — it’s the one I think about most. The headline items:
Resilience: multi-AZ MongoDB and Kafka, circuit breakers (Resilience4j on the gateway), automated DLQ replay, DR runbooks with documented RTO/RPO. Security: Vault-backed secrets, mTLS between gateway and downstream, rate limiting per principal/route, WAF, PII masking extended beyond kas-iam, a real penetration test, and a Cambodia data-protection compliance review. Observability beyond logs: OpenTelemetry traces, Prometheus + Grafana golden signals, formal SLOs (we have SLA targets but not SLOs), synthetic monitoring from regional vantage points, and an actual on-call rotation rather than Slack-only alerting. Performance: load testing with k6 or Gatling, a capacity plan sized to provinces × users × forms/day, CDN, MongoDB read replicas, Redis cluster mode, a connection-pooling sweep. Data governance: enforce Schema Registry contracts on kas.* topics, adopt one migration tool with idempotency tests, define retention policies, and inventory PII. DX & CI/CD: split CI matrices, contract tests at the gateway boundary, ephemeral pre-merge environments, branch protection and conventional commits, an internal developer portal. Frontend & mobile: offline-first hardening with proven sync conflict handling, low-bandwidth optimizations, Khmer language QA, and WCAG AA for backoffice tools used by government staff. Operational readiness: a real tenant model (province → district → commune as first-class citizens), feature flags for staged regional rollout, bulk import/export tooling for legacy records, training materials, and helpdesk integration. Phase 2, if it happens There’s a proposal on the table to generalize KAS beyond agriculture into a multi-industry data-entry backbone. We’ve done the preparation work — catalogued every place the codebase assumes “agriculture,” drafted the generic submission envelope:
{ "tenantId": "...", "industry": "...", "formId": "...", "schemaVersion": 1, "payload": { }, "attachments": [ ], "geo": { }, "submittedBy": "..." } …and confirmed Schema Registry can host industry-specific payload contracts. The architectural precondition is extracting the form engine out of kas-resource-api into a runtime form-definition service, with industry packs (form definitions + RBAC seed + reference data + optional industry service) as a first-class concept.
But that’s a leadership decision. Engineering’s recommendation is a small, scoped extraction of the form engine first — about a quarter, two or three engineers — before committing to a second industry.
Reflection The most useful thing I learned in Phase 1 isn’t on the report. It’s that picking one transformation pattern and applying it everywhere beats tailoring per-service. The observability rollout went fast precisely because we stopped re-litigating the design at each service. Same for the Docker Compose unification — once the canonical stack existed, every service became “fit into this” rather than “design your own.”
The risk for Phase 2, if leadership greenlights it, isn’t technical. It’s the temptation to keep adding capabilities in parallel with the multi-industry generalization. That’s the way I get a hybrid platform that does neither well. So Phase 2 should ship behind a feature flag, with one new industry as the proof, before anything else.
summary: Notes from four months re-architecting SAAMBAT/KAS at TSC: replacing the gateway, dropping internal E2EE, consolidating IAM, standardizing observability, and putting Kafka in the middle.
title: Re-engineering the KAS Platform — Phase 1
